title: SHE RECEIVED A GOLD NOSE RING AND BRACELETS BEFORE SHE EVER MET THE MAN SHE WOULD MARRY… BUT THE REAL MIRACLE WAS WHAT GOD SAW WHEN NOBODY WAS WATCHING.
paragraphs: SHE RECEIVED A GOLD NOSE RING AND BRACELETS BEFORE SHE EVER MET THE MAN SHE WOULD MARRY… BUT THE REAL MIRACLE WAS WHAT GOD SAW WHEN NOBODY WAS WATCHING.

Before Rebekah knew Isaac’s name, before she understood the journey ahead, and before she realized that one ordinary act of kindness would become part of a promise reaching generations into the future, God was already working. But the most astonishing part of Genesis 24 is not the gold she received. It is the God who was faithful long before she understood what was happening.

“And it came to pass, as the camels had done drinking, that the man took a golden earring of half a shekel weight, and two bracelets for her hands of ten shekels weight of gold.” — Genesis 24:22 (KJV)
She thought she was just going to get water.
That was all.
No announcement from heaven. No angel standing beside the well. No voice telling her that this particular afternoon would be remembered thousands of years later.
Just a young woman carrying a water jar, walking toward an ordinary responsibility.
And somewhere along the road, a stranger was praying.
What happened next would eventually connect her life to one of the most important promises in human history.
But before we get to the gold, the marriage, or the journey into an unknown future, there is something you need to understand.
Rebekah did not know she was standing in the middle of an answered prayer.
And perhaps that is why this story reaches so deeply into the human heart.
Because how many times have you walked through an ordinary day, exhausted by responsibilities, wondering whether God notices anything you do?
You get up. You work. You care for people. You give what little strength you have left. You pray prayers nobody hears. You carry burdens nobody sees.
And sometimes you wonder whether any of it matters.
Rebekah's story does not promise that every hidden sacrifice will produce a spectacular earthly reward.
It reveals something far more enduring.
God can be faithfully at work in circumstances that look completely ordinary.
And sometimes the people standing inside His providence are the last ones to recognize it.
Genesis 24 begins with an aging father.
Abraham had grown old. Sarah had died. And Isaac, the son through whom God had promised to continue Abraham's family line, was not yet married.
This was not simply a father worrying about his son's future.
God had promised Abraham that through his offspring all the nations of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 22:18).
The future of that promise mattered.
So Abraham entrusted his senior servant with a serious responsibility: travel to his relatives and seek a wife for Isaac.
But there was an important boundary.
Isaac was not to be taken back to Abraham's former homeland.
The servant would have to go, seek, and trust God with the outcome.
And if the woman refused to come?
Abraham made clear that she could not be forced.
Even before Rebekah enters the story, Scripture makes room for her decision.
Now imagine the servant arriving near the city of Nahor after a long journey.
Ten camels. Valuable goods. A responsibility that could not be fulfilled through human cleverness alone.
He stopped beside a well in the evening, at the time when women came to draw water.
And he prayed.
In Genesis 24:12, he said:
“O LORD God of my master Abraham, I pray thee, send me good speed this day, and shew kindness unto my master Abraham.” (KJV)
The Hebrew word translated here as “kindness” is חֶסֶד — ḥesed.
It is one of the richest words in the Old Testament.
Depending on its context, it speaks of steadfast love, covenant loyalty, faithfulness, and mercy.
The servant was not merely asking God to make his journey convenient.
He was appealing to the faithful character of the God who had made promises to Abraham.
And then he asked for a specific sign.
If he requested water from a young woman and she voluntarily offered water not only to him but also to his camels, he would recognize that response as an indication of God's guidance.
There is something beautiful here.
He did not ask for the wealthiest woman.
He did not ask for the most admired woman in the city.
He did not ask for someone whose appearance would impress Abraham's household.
He asked for a response that would reveal extraordinary hospitality.
And before he had finished speaking, Rebekah appeared.
Read that again.
Before he had finished speaking.
Genesis 24:15 records that Rebekah came out carrying her water jar.
The narrator immediately identifies her family connection to Abraham's relatives, something the servant had not yet learned.
He ran to meet her and asked for a little water.
She gave him a drink.
Then she said something he had specifically prayed to hear.
“I will draw water for thy camels also, until they have done drinking.” — Genesis 24:19 (KJV)
Do not rush past those words.
Ten camels.
Not one.
Ten.
Camels can consume substantial amounts of water, especially after traveling. Scripture does not tell us precisely how much water Rebekah drew, so we should not invent a dramatic number.
But it does tell us that she kept drawing until the animals had finished drinking.
That was no tiny favor.
She hurried. She emptied her pitcher. She ran back to the well. She drew again.
And again.
The stranger had asked for a drink.
Rebekah offered considerably more.
Not because she knew he carried jewelry.
Not because she knew he represented a wealthy household.
Not because she knew he had prayed for someone like her.
She simply responded with remarkable generosity.
And the servant watched.
Genesis 24:21 says he remained silent, observing her, seeking to understand whether the LORD had made his journey successful.
Picture that moment.
A young woman working beside a well.
A stranger quietly watching.
Camels drinking.
Water splashing against stone.
No crowd applauding.
No public recognition.
No one telling Rebekah that her actions would one day appear in the Bible.
And yet her kindness was becoming part of a much larger story.
There is a lesson here for everyone who feels invisible.
The mother caring for her children while quietly struggling with exhaustion.
The father working long hours and wondering whether his sacrifices mean anything.
The believer who continues praying even when the answers seem delayed.
The person who chooses integrity when dishonesty would be easier.
The Christian who serves without recognition.
You may not see the significance of every faithful decision.
But unseen does not mean meaningless.
Jesus would later teach that even giving a cup of cold water in His name matters to God (Matthew 10:42).
That does not mean kindness purchases divine favor.
It means the God who sees the heart does not measure faithfulness by the applause it receives.
And then came the gold.
Genesis 24:22 describes a gold nose ring weighing half a shekel and two gold bracelets weighing ten shekels.
The King James Version calls the first ornament a “golden earring,” but the Hebrew word is נֶזֶם — nezem, which can refer to a ring worn in the nose or ear.
The later description in Genesis 24:47 places this particular ornament on Rebekah's nose, which is why many modern translations correctly identify it as a nose ring.
The bracelets are called צְמִידִים — ṣemidim, ornaments worn around the wrists or arms.
These were valuable gifts, not ordinary trinkets.
And the timing matters.

Genesis 24:22 records the servant taking out the jewelry after the camels finished drinking. Genesis 24:23 then records his question about her family. Later, when recounting the encounter in Genesis 24:47, he describes asking her identity and then placing the jewelry on her.
The accounts should be read together rather than turned into a rigid sequence Scripture does not fully settle.
What is clear is astonishing enough.
Rebekah received valuable marriage-related gifts before she had ever met Isaac.
She had not seen his face.
She had not heard his voice.
She had not sat beside him.
She had not been promised a trouble-free future.
And the jewelry itself was not proof that every future decision had already been made for her.
The servant still had to speak with her family, explain his mission, and discover whether she would agree to go.
But the gold was a visible sign of the extraordinary invitation now unfolding.
And there is an even deeper detail that is easy to miss.
Rebekah did not receive the jewelry because she had successfully manipulated a wealthy stranger.
She had shown generosity before knowing what he could offer.
That distinction matters.
Because we live in a world that often teaches us to calculate every relationship.
What can this person give me?
Will helping them benefit my future?
Will anyone notice my sacrifice?
Is it worth being kind if nothing comes back?
But biblical kindness is not an investment strategy.
We do not love people to make God reward us with money, marriage, or promotion.
We love because God Himself is loving.
And when His grace transforms a heart, generosity becomes an expression of that transformation.
Rebekah's actions are worth admiring.
But they are not a formula for obtaining wealth.
They are part of a historical account showing how God's faithfulness unfolded through real people, real choices, and ordinary acts of hospitality.
Now watch what happens when she returns home.
Genesis 24:30 describes her brother Laban noticing the nose ring and bracelets and hearing her account of the stranger.
He ran out to meet the servant.
The household welcomed him.
Food was placed before him.
But the servant refused to eat until he had explained why he had come.
He told them about Abraham.
He told them about Isaac.
He told them about the journey.
He told them about his prayer.
And he told them how Rebekah had appeared before he had finished praying.
Then he bowed his head and worshiped the LORD.
Why?
Because he recognized God's faithful guidance.
The story was never ultimately about jewelry.
The servant's response was worship.
The gifts were significant, but God was greater than the gifts.
And that is where this ancient account begins to confront something painfully modern.
How many of us are so consumed with what we want God to give us that we have stopped seeking God Himself?
We want the relationship.
The breakthrough.
The financial relief.
The restored family.
The opportunity.
The answer.
And those desires are not automatically wrong.
But what happens when the gift becomes more important than the Giver?
What happens when our prayers become nothing more than demands for the life we think we deserve?
What happens when we begin treating God like a transaction?
We obey, so He must pay.
We give, so He must multiply our money.
We pray, so He must remove every difficulty.
We serve, so He must make us successful.
That is not the Gospel.
That is a bargain we have attempted to make with heaven.
And God has never needed our bargains.
He calls us to trust His character.
The same Hebrew word, ḥesed, appears again in Genesis 24:27 as the servant praises God for His kindness and faithfulness.
The focus remains on the LORD.
Not human deserving.
Not a secret formula.
Not a guarantee of earthly prosperity.
The faithful God of Abraham was keeping His promise.
But the story still had one essential question to answer.
Would Rebekah go?
When the family proposed delaying her departure, the servant asked not to be detained.
And then the family called Rebekah herself.
Genesis 24:58 records the question:
“Wilt thou go with this man?”
Her answer was simple.
“I will go.”
In Hebrew, her response is אֵלֵךְ — ʾēlēḵ.
“I will go.”
Two words in English.
One Hebrew verb.
A life-changing decision.
Imagine what that meant.
Leaving familiar surroundings.
Leaving the people she knew.
Traveling toward a man she had never met.
Entering a household whose future she could not fully predict.
Scripture does not tell us everything Rebekah felt in that moment.
It does not say she was fearless.
It does not tell us whether her heart raced, whether she struggled to sleep, or whether she imagined what Isaac might be like.
We should not pretend to know the emotions the Bible leaves unspoken.
But we do know her answer.
“I will go.”
And those words carry tremendous weight.
Not because every Christian should imitate her circumstances by making sudden marriage decisions.
Not because uncertainty automatically means God is directing us.
And certainly not because someone who claims to have heard from God has the right to pressure another person into a relationship.
Rebekah was asked.
Rebekah answered.
Her consent mattered.
Her decision became part of the unfolding story.
And for the person reading this who has been afraid to take a faithful step because the future is uncertain, there is something worth considering.
Faith does not mean pretending to know everything tomorrow will bring.
Faith means trusting the God who has revealed Himself to be faithful, while making wise and responsible decisions in the light He has given.
Sometimes obedience requires courage.
Sometimes it requires patience.
Sometimes it means going.
And sometimes it means refusing to move until what is being asked can be tested against God's Word.
Not every open door comes from God.
Not every attractive offer is His will.
Not every person who promises you a beautiful future is trustworthy.
But the LORD is trustworthy.
And His Word gives us a foundation stronger than our feelings.
Rebekah eventually arrived in the land where Isaac lived.
Genesis 24:63 tells us that Isaac had gone into the field toward evening.
He lifted his eyes and saw camels approaching.
Rebekah lifted her eyes and saw Isaac.
The man she had not met was finally before her.
She asked the servant who he was.
The servant answered that he was his master.
And Rebekah took her veil and covered herself.
Then the servant told Isaac everything that had happened.
Genesis 24:67 brings the account to its tender conclusion.
Isaac brought Rebekah into Sarah's tent.
She became his wife.
He loved her.
And he was comforted after his mother's death.
Do you see the quiet beauty?
The story began with an aging father and a family promise.
It moved through a servant's prayer.
A young woman's hospitality.
A journey of faith.
A voluntary decision.
And it ended with love and comfort in a household that had known grief.
But Genesis does not allow us to turn this marriage into a fairy tale where every sorrow disappears.
Later chapters reveal that Isaac and Rebekah experienced infertility, family conflict, parental favoritism, and painful divisions involving their sons.
Their marriage was real.
Their family was imperfect.
And God's faithfulness continued even through human weakness.
That is important because some people have been taught that being in God's will means everything will become easy.
That the right marriage will never hurt.
That the right decision will never involve disappointment.
That obedience guarantees a smooth road.
But the Bible tells the truth about people.
Even the people through whom God advances His purposes struggle, sin, suffer, and need mercy.
Rebekah was not a flawless heroine.
Isaac was not a flawless husband.
Their descendants were not flawless people.
And yet God's promise continued.
Now we come to the part of this story that reaches far beyond the well.
Because if we stop at the nose ring, the bracelets, and the marriage, we have missed the greatest treasure.
Through Isaac and Rebekah came Jacob.
Through Jacob came the twelve tribes of Israel.
Through Judah's line, according to the flesh, came Jesus Christ, as Matthew 1 and the wider biblical witness testify.
The promise made to Abraham was moving forward.
And that promise ultimately finds its fulfillment in Christ.
Galatians 3:16 directs our attention to Abraham's offspring and identifies Christ as the central fulfillment of the promise.
The blessing was never meant to terminate in one prosperous household.
God's redemptive purpose was reaching toward the nations.
Toward sinners.
Toward broken people.
Toward people who would never have stood beside Rebekah's well but who would desperately need the grace of the God she served.
Toward you.
Toward me.
And suddenly the story becomes much bigger than a young woman receiving gold.
Because there is another Bridegroom revealed in Scripture.
Jesus Christ.
The New Testament describes Christ as the Bridegroom and His redeemed people as His bride (Ephesians 5:25–27; Revelation 19:7–9).
This does not mean that every detail of Genesis 24 is a hidden code about Jesus.
We must not force meanings onto the passage that its author did not establish.
But when we read Genesis within the whole story of Scripture, we can recognize the magnificent direction of God's promises.
The line of Abraham leads us toward the Savior.
And the language of bridegroom and bride later reveals the covenant love of Christ for His people.
There is, however, a profound difference.
Rebekah received gold from a servant representing a wealthy household.
But the Church was not redeemed by silver or gold.
Listen to 1 Peter 1:18–19:

“Forasmuch as ye know that ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold, from your vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers; But with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot.” (KJV)
There it is.
The gold in Genesis was valuable.
But it could not redeem a single soul.
The blood of Jesus can.
And now the question is no longer whether you have received something beautiful from God.
The question is whether you have received the Savior Himself.
Because some of us have spent years collecting things that look like blessings while our hearts remain distant from the One who gives life.
We have built careers but neglected prayer.
Protected reputations while hiding sin.
Filled our homes with possessions while starving our souls of Scripture.
Learned how to look strong while quietly collapsing inside.
We know how to smile for photographs.
We know how to tell people we are fine.
We know how to post a Bible verse while refusing to surrender the bitterness that is consuming us.
And sometimes we become so skilled at appearing spiritually healthy that we stop admitting how badly we need Jesus.
But He already knows.
He knows the sin you regret.
The compromise you keep excusing.
The resentment you have rehearsed for years.
The secret you hope nobody discovers.
The prayer you stopped praying because disappointment became too painful.
And He does not call you to pretend.
He calls you to repent and believe the Gospel.
The Greek word commonly translated “repent” in the New Testament is μετανοέω — metanoeō.
It speaks of a change of mind and turning from sin toward God.
Repentance is not merely feeling emotional for a few minutes.
It is not posting a religious comment and returning unchanged to deliberate disobedience.
It is a real turning of the heart toward the Lord, made possible by His grace.
And the good news is that Jesus Christ did not come to save people who had already made themselves righteous.
He came to save sinners.
He lived without sin.
He died for our sins.
He was buried.
He rose again on the third day, according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
And everyone who turns to Him in faith finds a Savior who is sufficient.
Not because we have earned Him.
Not because our good deeds outweigh our failures.
But because salvation is God's gift of grace through faith in Jesus Christ (Ephesians 2:8–9).
He is not for sale.
His grace is not a premium membership.
His mercy does not come with a monthly price.
And the cross is not a business transaction.
Because genuine Gospel work should invite generosity without confusing financial support with salvation, spiritual worth, or obedience to God.
The apostle Paul wrote:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7 (KJV)
Notice those words.
Not grudgingly.
Not under compulsion.
From the heart.
Giving can glorify God when it flows from faith, love, gratitude, and a sincere desire to serve others.
Supporting the spread of biblical truth can be a beautiful expression of Christian generosity.
Your responsibilities to your local church, family, and those in genuine need still matter.
And no faithful ministry should make you feel that Christ's approval depends on sending it money.
At Gospel Warrior, we want the invitation to be something better than pressure.
We want it to be an opportunity to participate.
Because there are people who are desperate for the Word of God.
People who have not opened a Bible in years.
People whose marriages are unraveling.
People who feel ashamed to enter a church.
People who have been wounded by religious hypocrisy.
People who are curious about Jesus but do not know where to begin.
People who need more than a motivational sentence.
They need Scripture.
They need sound teaching.
They need the Gospel of repentance, forgiveness, reconciliation, and new life in Christ.
And this is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to replace the local church.
Not to sell salvation.
Not to make merchandise of people's pain.
But to help place biblical truth, Christian encouragement, and discipleship resources before people who need them.
That library is part of our desire to make Christian learning and spiritual nourishment more accessible.

If you have been looking for resources to help you study Scripture, grow in prayer, understand the Gospel, strengthen your walk with Christ, or encourage someone who is struggling, we invite you to explore what is available.
And if this ministry has encouraged you, and you are financially able, please consider becoming a monthly supporter.
It is not a substitute for every other form of Christian giving, nor is it a requirement for glorifying God.
But it can be one meaningful way to glorify Him through generosity and partnership in Gospel-centered work.
These products are not the reason anyone should follow Jesus.
You are welcome here.
The Gospel is still free.
The Scripture is still for you.
The invitation to grow in Christ is still for you.
And there are other ways to help.
Not merely because it might receive attention, but because someone among your family, friends, and acquaintances may need to encounter the truth it contains.
Perhaps there is a person who believes their life is too ordinary for God to notice.
Someone who thinks their past has disqualified them from grace.
Someone who has confused material prosperity with God's approval.
Someone who needs to understand that the greatest gift God gives is not a relationship, a financial blessing, or an easier life.
It is His Son.
And before you leave, I want to ask you something personal.
Not about Rebekah.
Not about her jewelry.
Not even about Isaac.
About you.
What is the ordinary place in your life where you are finding it hardest to trust God right now?
Is it your marriage?
Your family?
Your finances?
Your future?
Your battle with temptation?
Your struggle to forgive?
Your fear that you have wasted too many years?
You do not have to tell the whole world every private detail.
But you also do not have to pretend that the struggle is not real.
Someone reading may need the encouragement of knowing they are not the only one still learning to trust Him.
But remember: a comment is not a confession that earns forgiveness. A public response cannot replace personal repentance and faith.
The Lord hears you even when you cannot find the courage to say a word online.
Now, return with me one final time to that ancient well.
The sun is beginning to set.
The camels are drinking.
A young woman is carrying water.
A servant is watching in astonishment.
Gold will soon appear.
A journey will follow.
A marriage will begin.
Generations will come and go.
And eventually, through the promised family line, the Savior will enter the world.
Rebekah could not have understood the full sweep of that story while drawing water.
Neither can you see the full story of your life from where you stand today.
But you can know the One in whom God's promises find their fulfillment.
You can trust Jesus Christ.
You can turn from sin.
You can receive forgiveness.
You can walk in newness of life.
And you can stop measuring God's love by whether He has placed gold in your hands.
Because the greatest evidence of His love is not what you possess.
It is what Christ accomplished on the cross.
That is where our theme finds its deepest meaning.
Not because Rebekah herself was involved in a scandal. Genesis 24 makes no such claim.
But because the greater biblical story is filled with sinful, fractured, imperfect human beings whom God did not abandon to their rebellion.
And in Jesus Christ, the scandal of our sin meets the astonishing grace of God.
He does not merely decorate the old life.
He makes sinners new.
He does not merely cover our shame with something expensive.
He bears our sin and offers us forgiveness.
He does not promise that every chapter will be painless.
He promises that those who belong to Him will never be separated from His love (Romans 8:38–39).
And that is better than gold.
So the next time you feel overlooked, remember the well.
The next time you are tempted to measure your value by what someone gives you, remember the cross.
The next time you fear that your past is too ugly for redemption, remember the Savior who came to seek and save the lost.
And the next time you do something good that nobody notices, remember that faithfulness does not become worthless simply because it is unseen.
You may be standing in an ordinary moment.
You may be carrying an ordinary burden.
You may be doing an ordinary act of love.
You may have no idea what tomorrow holds.
But the God who kept His promise to Abraham has revealed His faithfulness supremely in Jesus Christ.
Hold fast to Him.
Because the most important part of your story will never be the gold you were given, the people who noticed you, or the doors that opened.
It will be whether you came to know the One who gave Himself to save you.

Rebekah went to the well carrying an empty jar. She left with a story she could never have imagined. But you can come to Jesus carrying a lifetime of sin and shame—and find a Savior whose grace is greater than everything you brought.
